name: portfolio-website
description: Personal site: a vintage room, SaahilOS, projects and a blog

readme.html:
portfolio-website

Saahil Sanganeriya's personal site. On a desktop, it opens on a vintage room built in Blender; the CRT on the desk runs SaahilOS, a small retro desktop. Every post, project and app has its own address, and opening one loads the room and opens that window on the monitor; there are no plain pages. Phones get the room at a lighter tier; a browser without WebGL gets SaahilOS on a drawn monitor. The site is built with Astro, MDX content collections, React (SaahilOS) and three.js (the room), and deploys to Vercel.

Based on Henry Heffernan's portfolio, heavily edited. Ideas from Alana Goyal's site. See Credits.

Run it

Node 22.12 or later.

npm install
npm run dev        # http://localhost:4321

Preview on the devbox

The devbox keeps a dev server of main running at 127.0.0.1:4321 (systemd user unit personal-website-preview.service). To see it from a laptop, open a tunnel and keep it running:

ssh -N -L 4321:127.0.0.1:4321 saahil-devbox

Then open http://localhost:4321.

Add a post in one step

Create src/content/blog/<slug>.mdx with this frontmatter and commit. The file name is the address: /blog/<slug> opens the post in its own window on the monitor, and the post joins the Writing window and /rss.xml.

---
title: The title of the post
date: 2026-10-12          # the day it is first published; never backdate
summary: One or two sentences for the post list, RSS and link previews.
tags: [film]
draft: false              # true: shows in `npm run dev` only
# film:                   # only for a film review
#   title: La La Land
#   year: 2016
#   rating: 5             # 0.5 to 5, in halves
#   letterboxd: https://letterboxd.com/saahilsan/film/la-la-land/
---

The post, in Markdown. An `<aside>` becomes a sidenote in the margin.

Add a project

Create src/content/projects/<slug>.mdx. It appears in the Projects window, and /projects/<slug> opens it.

---
title: An example project
summary: One line, 140 characters at most.
year: 2026
years: 2025–2026          # optional, shown instead of year
status: shipped           # shipped | research | archived
role: Designer and engineer
team: solo                # or "team of 4; I built the ingest service"
stack: [TypeScript, Astro]
featured: true            # featured projects come first, by `order`
order: 3
links:                    # each optional: repo, paper, demo, page, pypi
  repo: https://github.com/saahilsanganeriya/portfolio-website
# cover: ../../assets/projects/example.jpg
# coverAlt: What the image shows.
---

The write-up.

Add photos in one step

Put the photos in a folder (JPEG, PNG, WebP, AVIF or TIFF; export HEIC as JPEG first) and run:

npm run photos:ingest -- path/to/photos --series 2019 --year 2019    # both optional

For each photo it applies the camera's rotation, strips every metadata block (EXIF with GPS location, XMP, IPTC, ICC), writes AVIF and WebP copies at 480, 960 and 1600 px and the original size (up to 2400 px) on the long edge into src/assets/photography/<name>/, and writes src/content/photography/<name>.yaml. The file name is the <name>. Running it again skips photos already in, and never overwrites an entry, so edit the entries freely:

file: "../../assets/photography/amer-fort/2400.webp"   # written by the script
title: "amer fort"
year: 2019                # default: --year, else the photo's own capture year, else this year
place: "Amer Fort"        # optional
series: "2019"            # default: --series, else the year; name a series by year, place or what the photos share
caption: "Amer Fort beyond a wall, in black and white."   # one line; it is also the alt text, so say what is in it
featured: false           # the favourites
onWall: false             # framed on the room's print wall; it has five frames, and favourites fill the rest
order: 20                 # optional; lower comes first

src/content/photography/ is for photography only, never photos of me. Those go through --me:

npm run photos:ingest -- ~/photos/me --me

which writes the sizes into src/assets/me/<name>/ and adds { "file": "<name>", "alt": "", "use": "about" } to src/content/me.json. Write the alt text and set use (opening, about, thread or resume) before building: an empty alt fails the build. A photo of me appears only where it is placed beside text: in an .mdx page with <MePhoto file="<name>" side="right" />, or in a story chapter with photo: "<name>".

Update the favourite films (the posters) in one step

With a Letterboxd export unzipped, run npm run favorites -- <export folder> and commit src/content/favorites.json.

The posters in the room are the four favourite films on the Letterboxd profile, in profile order. They are also the "Four favourites" at the top of the Films window. Letterboxd answers a request for a profile page with HTTP 403, and the RSS feed does not include the favourites. So the source is the account export: its profile.csv has a "Favorite Films" column with four boxd.it links. In full, after a change on Letterboxd:

  1. Export the data (Letterboxd, Settings, Data, Export your data) and unzip it.
  2. Run npm run favorites -- <export folder>. The script follows each boxd.it link to its film page (browser User-Agent, 10 s timeout, one request each 2 s, about 15 s in total) and writes src/content/favorites.json: { source, updated, films: [{ slug, title, year, director, poster }] }. If a request fails, the file does not change and the script exits 1.
  3. Commit src/content/favorites.json.

A favourite with hand-drawn art has poster: "/room/posters/<slug>.avif". A .ktx2 file with the same name is next to it for three.js. A favourite without art has poster: null, and the room draws a typographic poster for it with renderPoster(film) from src/lib/posters.ts. That function returns a self-contained SVG string (the text is in outlines, so an <img> or a texture shows it without web fonts). To add hand-drawn art, add a design to scripts/posters/designs.mjs with the film's slug as its id. Then run npm run posters -- <slug>, npm run posters:runtime -- <slug> and npm run favorites -- <export folder>. The art for films that are no longer favourites stays in blender/posters/.

Content

Collection Files Addresses (each opens its window on the monitor)
projects src/content/projects/<slug>.mdx /projects, /projects/<slug>
blog src/content/blog/<slug>.mdx /blog, /blog/<slug>, /rss.xml
pages src/content/pages/{about,resume}.mdx /about, /resume
story src/content/story/<nn>-<slug>.mdx /story (The Thread)
photography src/content/photography/<name>.yaml (npm run photos:ingest) the photography exhibit (SaahilOS, the room)

The schemas are in src/content.config.ts. Every entry is also served as static JSON at /content/<collection>/<slug>.json ({ data, html }), which SaahilOS reader windows load.

Films come from the Letterboxd diary of saahilsan. The archive is the export in src/data/letterboxd/ (diary, ratings, reviews, watched; the Tags column is removed). /api/films.json, the only server route, merges the public RSS feed over it per film and watched date, at most once an hour (Vercel ISR), at most one Letterboxd request per 2 s. When the feed fails, it serves the archive and the last good copy. src/content/films.json is the same merge, written by each build as the static fallback. Set FILMS_PRIVATE_NAMES (comma-separated, in Vercel) to drop the text of any live review that names one of those people.

Scripts

Command What it does
npm run dev Dev server at http://localhost:4321.
npm run build Writes src/content/films.json (archive + Letterboxd feed), then builds into dist/ and .vercel/output/.
npm run preview Serves the last build from .vercel/output/, /api/films.json included (astro preview does not support the Vercel adapter).
npm run check Type-checks the project (astro check).
npm run test:e2e Playwright tests in tests/*.spec.ts. They build with SAMPLES=1 (draft posts included) and serve the build themselves.
node scripts/check-routes.mjs Builds, then checks every address: each entry's page is the room opening its window, with its JSON body; no page exists beyond those, /os and /story (framed inside the room) and /404; each page has a title, description, og:title, og:image and one <h1>; no internal link is broken. --samples includes draft posts.
npm run photos:ingest -- <folder> Strips all metadata from the photos in a folder, writes AVIF and WebP sizes, and adds an entry per photo (see "Add photos in one step").
npm run films Writes src/content/films.json: the archive and the cached copy, with the Letterboxd feed merged over them. When the feed fails, it keeps the cached copy and exits 0.
npm run posters [-- <slug> ...] Draws the hand-drawn posters into blender/posters/ (SVG and 2048-px PNG).
npm run posters:runtime [-- <slug> ...] Writes the runtime copies of the favourites' posters to public/room/posters/ (AVIF 683×1024 and KTX2 512×768, 120 KB or less each).
npm run favorites -- <export folder> Writes src/content/favorites.json from a Letterboxd export's profile.csv.
node scripts/posters/glyphs.mjs Writes src/lib/poster-glyphs.ts, the glyph outlines renderPoster uses. Run it again only when the fonts or the character sets change.
npm run measure:payload, npm run measure:fps Measure the room's payload (the initial load until the room is interactive, and what a visit loads on demand) and its frame rate in each framing.

Deploy

Vercel, through @astrojs/vercel. Every page is prerendered. A route that must run on request sets export const prerender = false; Vercel then caches it with ISR for at most an hour.

The Vercel project (portfolio-website) is not connected to the GitHub repository, so a push does not deploy. From a checkout, npx vercel link --yes --project portfolio-website once, then npx vercel deploy --prod --yes; Vercel runs npm run build itself.

Design

Warm light in a dark room, and one thread. Colours: ink #14110F (background), walnut #3B2A1E, paper #EDE4D3 (text), dust #A89F91 (secondary text), thread #B4442C (the one accent; never for text), projector #9DB4C0 (the beam and the CRT only). Type: Newsreader for headings and essays, IBM Plex Sans for the interface, IBM Plex Mono for code. Reading windows have no effects over the text.

Credits

Based on Henry Heffernan's portfolio, heavily edited: the room scene comes from portfolio-website (MIT) and SaahilOS from portfolio-inner-site (used with his permission). Ideas from Alana Goyal's site (MIT). The licence texts are in NOTICE. Every third-party asset, with its source and licence, is listed in blender/ASSETS.md and on /credits.
